title: Journalism, speeches, letters and life writing
summary: The conventions of news reports, opinion pieces, features, speeches, open letters, blogs and memoirs, and how writers use or bend them.

keyterms.definition: The title of a news or feature article, designed to grab attention and frame the story.
The opening paragraph of a news story, summarising the key facts.
An opinion article by a named writer, arguing a personal position on an issue.
An unsigned opinion piece expressing a publication's official view.
A longer, in-depth article that explores a topic with description, interviews and a more personal style.
A striking quotation enlarged within an article's layout to draw readers in.
A letter addressed to a person or group but published for a wide audience, usually to make a public argument.
A non-fiction account of part of the writer's life, shaped and selected like a story.
An online text, usually informal and personal, published in regular posts that invite reader interaction.
Identifying the source of a quotation or claim, e.g. 'according to police', which affects credibility.
The line naming the writer of an article.
An opposing view a writer raises in order to refute it, strengthening their own position.

questions.prompt: Which is the key difference between an editorial and an op-ed?
options: An editorial gives the publication's unsigned view; an op-ed is signed by an individual writer
questions.explanation: Authorship affects ethos: institutional authority versus personal voice.

questions.text: The opening paragraph of a news story that summarises key facts is the ___.
questions.explanation: The lead (or lede) answers who, what, when and where as quickly as possible.

questions.prompt: Headline: "MOTHER'S AGONY AS HOSPITAL TURNS HER AWAY". Which feature makes it sensational?
questions.explanation: Emotive vocabulary and a human-interest frame make the headline dramatic and sympathetic.

questions.statement: "Protesters were injured" and "Police injured protesters" give different impressions of responsibility.
questions.explanation: The passive voice can hide who acted; choice of voice frames blame.

questions.prompt: Match the journalistic feature to its function.

pairs.right: Grabs attention and frames the story

questions.explanation: Each feature shapes credibility, attention or framing.

questions.prompt: An op-ed writer says: "Some will argue the tax hurts small businesses. But the evidence from three cities shows the opposite." What technique is this?
questions.explanation: Anticipating objections and rebutting them makes the writer seem fair and confident.

questions.text: A longer, in-depth article with interviews and descriptive scene-setting is a ___ article.
questions.explanation: Features use narrative techniques more than hard news does.

questions.statement: Attribution such as "sources suggest" is as strong as naming a specific expert.
questions.explanation: Vague attribution weakens credibility; named, qualified sources strengthen ethos.

questions.prompt: A feature article opens with a vivid scene of a fisherman mending nets at dawn before discussing overfishing. Why?
options: To humanise a large issue and draw readers in
To give the main statistics first
questions.explanation: Scene-setting openings are a feature convention that builds engagement before argument.

questions.prompt: Order the typical structure of an op-ed.
items: Memorable conclusion or call to action
questions.explanation: This structure balances engagement, reasoning and persuasion.

questions.prompt: Why might an activist publish an open letter to a CEO rather than send a private one?
options: To build public pressure and reach supporters as well as the addressee
questions.explanation: An open letter has a dual audience: the named addressee and the public watching.

questions.text: A non-fiction account of part of the writer's own life is a ___.
questions.explanation: Memoirs select and shape experience; they are constructed like stories.

questions.statement: Because a memoir is non-fiction, it involves no choices about selection or narrative structure.
questions.explanation: Memoirists choose what to include, how to order it and how to present their past selves, so analyse them as crafted texts.

questions.prompt: A blog post ends: "What do you think? Tell me in the comments!" What does this reflect?
options: The interactive, community-building conventions of blogs
questions.explanation: Blogs invite participation, building a relationship between writer and readers.

questions.prompt: Match the text type to its typical register.
questions.explanation: Register follows audience and purpose; deviations are worth analysing.

questions.prompt: A memoir is written in present tense: "I am seven. The house smells of smoke." What is the effect?
options: It immerses the reader in the child's experience as if it is happening now
It shows the writer forgot grammar
It makes the text an advert
questions.explanation: Present tense creates immediacy and restricts the view to the child's perspective.

questions.text: A letter addressed to someone but published for the wider public is an ___ letter.
questions.explanation: Open letters use the letter form as a public platform.

questions.prompt: In a graduation speech, a principal tells a story about failing her own first exam. What is the main purpose of this anecdote?
options: To build connection and encourage resilience
questions.explanation: Self-deprecating anecdotes humanise speakers and model the message.

questions.statement: Speeches are written to be heard, so features like repetition, direct address and short sentences are especially important.
questions.explanation: Oral delivery shapes the conventions of the speech as a text type.

questions.prompt: A travel blogger lists "5 hidden beaches you NEED to visit". What does the listicle form suggest about audience?
options: Skimming online readers who want quick, shareable content
Readers who want a long novel
questions.explanation: Numbered lists, bold claims and capitals suit fast online reading and sharing.
